Skill pack for AI coding agents

Change what your agent reaches for.

Ask any coding agent for a landing page and you get the same one: Inter, a violet gradient, three equal cards, a spinner on a timer. frontend-design-pro is a pack it loads while it writes, so the defaults are different ones — and the output gets checked rather than hoped for.

Install it Route a request
$ npx skills add Krishna-Modi12/frontend-design-pro

One request, traced

  • 01 Trigger keywords match one skill — most specific wins
  • 02 That skill's declared core files load beside it
  • 03 Its reference material stays on disk until something needs it

A typical request loads 5,961–7,525 tokens, against 349,467 tokens of reference depth that stay on disk. That ratio is the whole architecture: a registry that routes, not a document that loads.

How it works

A registry that routes, checks that fail, gates that block.

This is not a prompt you paste. It is a router with depth behind it, and the output is held to constraints that run in CI rather than to advice that hopes to be followed.

1. Route

The agent holds one always-loaded registry, matches your request against trigger keywords, then opens exactly one of 19 skills plus the core files it declares. No keyword match, and it asks a question instead of guessing.

2. Check

What it writes is held to 60 machine-checked constraints (17 AST + 43 regex) — the first half walked through the TypeScript compiler, the second run as patterns. Ten deliberate anti-examples exist to prove the checks actually fire.

3. Gate

Nothing ships unless all 11 gates pass on a clean runner: compilation, both constraint suites, the test suite, the reference corpus, and a gate that recomputes every published figure.

The registry

Nineteen skills. Your request loads one.

Those 19 skills sit in front of 101 references, and a request opens one skill plus only the references it points at. Open any row for what it covers, what loads with it, what that costs, and the sentence that routes there — then send that sentence straight up to the router.

Output

Four pages the pack produced.

Two of them run here. The comparison between those two is the honest part of this site rather than the flattering part.

Earned

Bellwether A rehearsal tool for pending database migrations

Its brief asked for near-black with one bright accent — the exact look the pack's own wall refuses to produce unless a brief asks for it. So the page was permitted before it was designed, and the question became what it had to do to deserve the exemption: a cobalt at moderate chroma rather than an acid neon, one hue across every neutral, every colour pair measured on all three of its surfaces. Six pairs failed the first pass and were corrected before it shipped.

Open Bellwether
Permitted

Nexus A fictional AI analytics platform

The same exemption, taken and left there. Its brief asked for near-black and acid green and got exactly that: a WebGL hero, an asymmetric bento grid, a validated form, every constraint green, no rule broken — and a page that looks like every other generated developer-tool site on the internet. It is kept unchanged because it is the control.

Held to the same constraints as everything else, but stub-typed rather than installed, so there is no build to serve — this is a capture from the source in the repository.

Not deployed

Auth form Validation wired to the fields it describes

The demo where the schema and the form are asserted to agree at compile time, after a type stub loose enough to accept anything once let them drift apart in silence.

Bellwether and Nexus are invented products. Neither is a real service, neither collects anything, and no figure on either page describes a real system. The pack is real; the companies are not.

The honest edge

What no gate in this repository can see.

A product claiming to verify design owes you the places the verification stops. Three of them:

A green run is not a good page

Every constraint the pack enforces is green on both demos above. The difference between them is in no rule, and no gate here can measure it. A gate can tell you a page broke no rule; it cannot tell you the page was designed.

The wall has an exemption in it

Three AI-design defaults — cream and serif and terracotta, near-black with a single acid accent, broadsheet hairline columns — are banned unless the brief asks for them. Without that clause the rules would overrule the person using them. With it, a brief can walk an agent straight back into the default the wall was written to prevent.

Nothing renders anything

Every gate reads source. None starts a browser, and the gap is not theoretical: a stylesheet that silently did nothing, a page that scrolled sideways on a phone, and a chart hidden from screen readers but still in the tab order all passed a fully green chain.

Install

One command, or a pinned archive.

Both routes give you the same skills. Only one of them is a version.

Install from the default branch

It detects the agents you have installed and wires the pack into each. It arrives as one skill, which is the shape this needs: the router lands with core/ and every skill beside it, so routing still works.

$ npx skills add Krishna-Modi12/frontend-design-pro

This route tracks the default branch, not a release. You get whatever is on main at that moment, which is not the artifact the gates signed off. And do not pass --full-depth: it installs every skill as a peer instead of one router over the rest, and the routing is the product.

Take the gated artifact instead

The archive is built only when every gate passes, carries a version stamp, and has each path inside it checked to resolve.

$ gh release download --repo Krishna-Modi12/frontend-design-pro --pattern '*.skill'

Browse the latest release

Adapters that ship inside the pack

The archive carries host-specific adapters, so the same rules reach agents that do not read the skill format directly.
